newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's conservatives under attack as polls near.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's conservatives under attack as polls near.

text.p: Religious fanatics? Closet fascists? Government stooges?
The barbs against Mexico's conservatives may be hurled by political opponents but they seem to be hitting home.
A year ago, the right-wing National Action Party (PAN) was riding high. A string of election victories had party chiefs talking of when, rather than if, they would be running Mexico.
Now, just over two weeks before elections for the congress they had hoped to control, PAN support is fading.

In Mexico City, the latest polls show the PAN mayoral candidate slumping to third place, way behind the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) and lower even than the unpopular ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

In the northern industrial state of Nuevo Leon -- supposedly fertile ground for the PAN's pro-business, anti- corruption stance -- the party's candidate for governor, Fernando Canales Clariond, has seen a big initial poll lead over the PRI evaporate. Some say Canales could now lose.

PAN officials predict they will still be the biggest opposition party in Congress after the July 6 elections. They promise to improve on the 25.8 percent national showing they managed in the last congressional vote in 1994.
But party leaders no longer talk of winning a congressional majority, or even of being the biggest single party in the lower house, as they did a year ago.
What has changed?

Voters are still angry that their standard of living has crashed in the wake of Mexico's disastrous 1994-5 economic crisis and remain determined to break the PRI's 68-year-old virtual monopoly of political power, polls show.
But political analysts say the left-wing PRD seems to be harvesting voter discontent more effectively than the conservatives.
The main reasons for the PAN's problems, they say, are threefold:
-- for the first time, the PAN are incumbents in various parts of the country and have to defend a record in government.

-- attacks by some PAN politicians on swearing in public, condoms and miniskirts have allowed critics to resurrect an old stereotype that the party is excessively moralistic and unhealthily close to the Catholic church.

-- the PAN's history of support for the 1988-94 government of Carlos Salinas and his reforms. Salinas is now in disgrace because of the corruption allegations and economic disaster that followed his administration.

-- the disastrous record of a PAN incumbent in the attorney-general's office in the first two years of the Zedillo administration, which ended with the firing of PAN Attorney-General Antonio Lozano and the arrest of one of his top officials.
"The PAN is paying the price for backing Carlos Salinas," political commentator Miguel Angel Granados Chapa told Reuters.
Granados Chapa said that the PRD was successfully reminding voters of its unyielding opposition to Salinas through its high-profile candidate for mayor of Mexico City, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas.
Most Mexicans believe Salinas only beat Cardenas in the 1988 presidential election with the help of massive electoral fraud, a charge the government denied.
Other critics emphasise the PAN's religious leanings.

"Mexican society seems determined not to jump back into the past," commentator Francisco Martin Moreno wrote in the newspaper Excelsior this week. "The marriage of the PAN with the (Catholic) church, the most retarded institution in Mexico, seems unfortunate as we face the next millenium."
The PAN dismisses such criticism as electorally motivated.

"There are many labels that have been placed upon the PAN today - too moralist, too far to the right, too close to Salinas," said leading PAN official and governor of Guanajuato state Vicente Fox in an interview with Reuters Financial TV.
"All of them have been with the intent of discouraging voters...Where we are having problems is Mexico City."
But the PRD -- which paid a heavy price for opposing Salinas with over 300 of its members killed in violence during his rule -- is telling voters it stuck to principles.
"Salinas hit us very hard, he wanted to destroy us," PRD national leader Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador told Reuters.
"We decided to resist...we made a lot of sacrifices but at the end of the day that is what is helping us most."
